newsitem.title: INDIA: India coalition impasse to hit oil firms, economy.
newsitem.headline: India coalition impasse to hit oil firms, economy.

text.p: The decision to defer an increase in oil prices by India's United Front, split on ways to plug a mounting oil subsidy bill, will pinch state-owned oil firms and the economy, officials said on Tuesday.
"It will lead to a catastrophe for the economy," said Y.R. Mehta, an independent oil analyst.
For the second time in three weeks the 15-party ruling coalition failed to reach a consensus on the politically sensitive issue and decided to meet again on June 27.
"Oil companies are already stretched and will again start borrowing. It will affect their cash flows and financial performance," Mehta said.
"It (the postponement) can't be indefinite," said an official of the state-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC), who asked not to be indentified.

The companies at the end of March were owed 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) from the oil pool account deficit, which represents money owed by the government to companies for selling below market prices.

The oil subsidy bill in fiscal 1997/98 totalled around 180 billion rupees -- which includes the cost of both products sold below market prices plus a cross-subsidisation element under which some products, like gasoline, are priced above market prices.
"The oil companies have to borrow more to fund the deficit," Sanjiv Patni, an analyst at securities firm W.I. Carr, told Reuters.
"Already the receivables (of the oil companies) are very high. The government has to do something to ease the situation, especially for Indian Oil Corp, which is stretched," he said.

IOC, the sole importer of crude into the country and owed around 100 billion rupees ($2.79 billion) by the government, has asked the Petroleum Ministry to put pressure on refiners to repay oustanding bills for feedstock supplied to them.
"We can go on maybe for just another two months like this," the IOC official said.
Some industry officials argue that a softening of global oil prices had given the government a breather.
But Carr's Patni said while the oil pool deficit was growing more slowly the cumulative deficit was still massive.
Leftwing parties in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's coalition have steadfastly opposed raising prices of some petroleum products such as kerosene and diesel to plug the mounting oil pool deficit.
"We want the government to see other options," D. Raja, a senior leader of Communist Party of India (CPI), told Reuters on Monday.
CPI's leftist cousin, the larger Communist Party of India (Marxist) CPI (M) has submitted an alternative plan to the Steering Committee on ways of avoiding a hike in oil prices.

The plan calls for the government to return to the state-run oil sector funds taken by earlier governments from the oil pool, when it was in surplus, as well as the elimination of customs and excise duties.

Last July the government raised the price of gasoline by 25 percent, and prices of high-speed diesel, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for cooking, paraffin wax and fuel oil by 30 percent. It was forced to scale back the rise in diesel prices to 15 percent after nationwide protests.
